rows.text:
Good question — it's actually an optical illusion, not a real size change. The Moon's angular size (how big it is on your retina) is essentially the same at the horizon as overhead; if you measure it with a camera or even just your thumb held at arm's length, it's the same. The leading explanation is called the 'Moon illusion': near the horizon, your brain sees the Moon next to distant trees, buildings, and the horizon line, which gives it cues of relative size and distance. Overhead, there's nothing to compare it to — just empty sky. Many researchers (going back to Kaufman & Rock) tie this to how we perceive the sky as a flattened dome: we judge horizon objects as farther away than zenith objects, so when something at the 'farther' horizon has the same apparent size as something overhead, the brain concludes it must actually be bigger. It's a perception effect in your visual system, not atmospheric magnification or an actual change in the Moon's distance.
